title: Calamari Ripieni
subtitle: squid stuffed with breadcrumbs, herbs, and capers, braised in tomato
excerpt: Calamari ripieni are whole squid tubes stuffed with a breadcrumb, parsley, caper, and Parmesan filling, then braised in tomato sauce until the squid is tender. The stuffing expands slightly as the squid cooks and soaks up the tomato. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Calamari ripieni (stuffed squid) is a dish of the southern Italian and Sicilian coast, documented from at least the 19th century. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), gives a recipe for stuffed squid braised in its own ink or tomato sauce. The preparation appears throughout coastal Campania, Sicily, and Puglia, with local variations in the stuffing. The Sicilian version typically adds pine nuts and raisins to the stuffing in keeping with the Arab-influenced agrodolce tradition; the Campanian version is plainer with breadcrumbs, anchovy, parsley, and capers. Both are braised in tomato sauce for a long enough time to tenderise the squid completely.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the braised stuffed squid in its sauce. Thaw and reheat gently over a low heat.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Stuff the squid up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate. Braise from cold, adding 10 minutes to the time.

glossaryTerms.definition: The body of a squid cleaned of its internal quill and organs, leaving a tube of firm, pale flesh. Available cleaned from fishmongers and supermarkets. For stuffing, choose large squid with tubes at least 10 cm long: small squid have less room for the filling and take less time to cook.

content.text: Calamari ripieni works on a counterintuitive principle: squid that is stuffed and then braised for a long time ends up tender, even though brief cooking of squid is usually the rule. The long, gentle braise in tomato sauce tenderises the squid beyond the rubber-band stage it passes through at the 10 to 15 minute mark, emerging at 45 minutes as something soft and yielding. The stuffing plumps up and absorbs the tomato, and the sauce thickens around everything.

items.prepNote: 4 large squid, cleaned, tubes and tentacles separated

content.text: Make the stuffing and fill the squid

Finely chop the squid tentacles. Mix with {{breadcrumbs-coarse}} of breadcrumbs, {{parmesan}} of Parmesan, {{capers}} of capers, {{parsley-flat}} of parsley, {{garlic}} of garlic (the stuffing portion), {{anchovy-fillets}} of anchovies, the beaten egg, and {{olive-oil}} of olive oil. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt. The mixture should be slightly damp and hold together.
Fill each squid tube two-thirds full with the stuffing using a small spoon. Do not pack too tightly. Secure each opening with a toothpick.
Heat the sauce olive oil in a large saute pan over a medium-high heat. Brown the stuffed squid tubes on all sides for about 3 minutes total. Remove and set aside.

In the same pan, add the sauce garlic and chilli flakes. Cook 1 minute. Add {{dry-white-wine}} of white wine and let it bubble for 1 minute. Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} of tinned tomatoes and crush them. Return the stuffed squid to the pan.

Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook on the lowest possible heat for 40 to 45 minutes until the squid is completely tender when pierced with a knife. Turn the squid once or twice during cooking. Remove the toothpicks before serving.
Serve the calamari with the tomato sauce spooned over and around, with good bread or alongside pasta.

items.symptom: Squid is tough and rubbery at serving time
items.cause: Braised for too short a time
items.fix: Squid goes through a tough stage at 15 to 25 minutes. Continue braising: at 40 minutes it will be tender. The low heat is important; a rapid simmer makes it tougher.

items.symptom: Stuffing bursts out of the tubes
items.fix: Fill to two-thirds only. The stuffing expands as it cooks. Toothpick sealing prevents the opening from coming apart.
Remove the squid at the end of cooking and reduce the sauce uncovered for 5 minutes before returning the squid to warm through.

content.text: Calamari ripieni is found along the southern Italian coast, from Naples through Calabria and into Sicily, with different stuffings by region. The Sicilian version adds raisins and pine nuts; the Campanian is plainer and more anchovy-forward. It is a home-cooking dish rather than a restaurant one: the long braise means it is cooked ahead and reheated, which suits a domestic kitchen well. It improves overnight and the sauce is even better the next day.
